## Ecommerce Website Development in Pune: Should You Build Your Own Online Store or Keep Selling Only on Marketplaces?

Sell on marketplaces first if you have no audience, a small catalogue and no one to run a store; build your own ecommerce website as soon as you have repeat customers, a brand people search for, or margins that the marketplace is eating. In practice most Pune sellers end up doing both, and the real decision is about what each channel is for: a marketplace rents you customers, your own store lets you keep them. This guide helps a seller, a manufacturer or a shop owner decide when to add an own-website channel, what it really involves, and how to avoid the two classic mistakes: building a store nobody visits, and staying on marketplaces long after they have stopped being worth it.

We write this as a team that builds stores. That is a bias, so we try to be fair to marketplaces. We do not quote marketplace commission rates, fee schedules or "average" conversion figures, because platforms change them often and we cannot source current numbers here. Where a number matters, we tell you how to get it from your own seller account.

### What each channel actually gives you

The two channels sell different things, and confusing them leads to bad decisions.

**A marketplace gives you demand you did not have to create.** Shoppers already arrive on Amazon, Flipkart, Meesho and similar platforms looking to buy. You list a product and can be in front of buyers quickly. In exchange, the platform controls the listing format, the search ranking, the pricing environment, the customer relationship and often the rules for returns and ratings.

**Your own store gives you control and the customer.** You decide the design, the product story, the pricing, the offers, the checkout and, importantly, you own the customer's contact details and order history (subject to data-protection duties). In exchange, you must bring the visitors yourself, through search, ads, social media, email, WhatsApp and word of mouth.

So the trade is simple: marketplaces rent you traffic; your own site makes you build it. Neither is better in general. Which is better for you, now, depends on where you are.

### The questions that decide it

Rather than a verdict, here are the questions. Answer them honestly.

#### Do people already search for your brand?

If shoppers type your brand name into Google or ask for you by name, they will look for your own site. Without one, you send them to a marketplace listing where competitors sit beside you. If nobody knows your brand yet, an own store has no natural visitors, and you will have to pay or work to create them.

#### Do customers buy more than once?

Repeat purchase is where an own store earns its keep. If your product is consumable, replenishable, gifted or collected, the cost of acquiring a customer once can be spread over many orders, and owning the relationship lets you reach them again by email or WhatsApp. If most customers buy a single product once, the economics of an own store depend heavily on cheap acquisition.

#### What is the marketplace taking from each sale?

Open your seller dashboard and total everything: the commission, fixed fees, shipping or fulfilment charges, return costs, advertising you pay to stay visible and any penalties. Then divide by the sale price. TODO: replace this with your own figures from the last three months of settlement reports. Many sellers find the real cost is larger than the headline commission, because advertising and returns are what keep a listing alive. Compare that total with what you would spend to acquire a customer on your own site.

#### Do you control your pricing and brand?

Marketplace price comparison is merciless: a competitor undercuts and the buyer sees both. If your products are branded, handmade, customised or hard to compare, an own store lets you tell a story the marketplace layout cannot. If you sell a commodity identical to a hundred others, the marketplace's search and trust may serve you better than your own site would.

#### Can you ship and support orders yourself?

An own store makes you responsible for everything the marketplace partly handled: packing, shipping, returns, customer questions, payment failures. Some marketplaces provide fulfilment. If you cannot yet pack and ship reliably, fix that first. A beautiful store that ships late damages your brand more than a marketplace listing does.

#### Do you have the time, or a team, to run it?

A store needs ongoing work: adding products, updating stock, answering messages, running campaigns, fixing issues. Our guide to [website maintenance plans](/blog/web-development-company-pune-website-maintenance-plan-what-to-include-2026/) describes the technical side. If nobody has the time, the store decays, and a neglected store can look worse than none.

### When marketplaces are the right primary channel

Marketplaces are the sensible main channel when you are testing whether a product sells at all, when the catalogue is small and commoditised, when shoppers search by product type rather than by brand, when you lack the budget to bring traffic to your own site, and when you want to learn from real buyers' reviews and questions before investing. Our [marketplace brand listing service](/services/marketplace-brand-listing/) exists because many Indian brands start this way and want the listings done properly.

### When an own store becomes worth building

An own store tends to make sense when several of these are true.

- Your brand has some recognition, so people search for it.
- Customers return, or could with a nudge.
- You have a catalogue where product stories, bundles or customisation matter.
- Marketplace costs and rules are squeezing margins or limiting what you can sell.
- You want customer data to run your own email and WhatsApp communication.
- You sell to businesses or in bulk, where marketplace formats fit poorly. Our guide to [wholesale and B2B ordering](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-wholesale-b2b-ordering-trade-pricing-2026/) covers what changes.
- You sell through other channels, such as a shop, Instagram, WhatsApp or sales visits, and want one place to take orders.

### The hybrid approach most sellers end up with

For many sellers the answer is not either-or. A common pattern is to use marketplaces for discovery and volume while using the own store for repeat customers, higher-margin or exclusive products, bundles and direct orders from social media and WhatsApp.

Be careful about channel conflict. If your own store is priced higher than the marketplace for the same item, shoppers who compare will buy on the marketplace. If you price lower on your own site, check the marketplace's rules, as some restrict undercutting. Many sellers solve this with exclusive bundles, extra products, better service, loyalty offers or early access on their own store, rather than a price fight.

Also check each marketplace's rules about taking customers off the platform. Most prohibit steering buyers to your own site through packaging inserts or messages in certain ways. Read the seller policies and follow them. A banned seller account is a high price for a small shortcut.

### What building an own store really involves

Many first-time sellers underestimate what a store needs. Here is the real list of workstreams.

**Platform choice.** Shopify, WooCommerce or a custom build, each with different costs and trade-offs. Our guide to [choosing between Shopify and WooCommerce](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-shopify-vs-woocommerce-platform-choice-2026/) compares them for Indian stores.

**Product data.** Titles, descriptions, images, variants, prices, stock, weights. This is where most launches stall, because marketplace listings are often thin. Our guide to [preparing product catalogue data](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-catalogue-data-preparation-2026/) explains the spreadsheet work.

**Product pages that convert.** A marketplace page borrows trust from the platform. Yours must earn it with clear photos, honest descriptions, delivery information, reviews and returns policy. See our [product page checklist](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-page-conversion-checklist-2026/).

**Checkout and payments.** Payment methods that Indian shoppers expect, clear delivery charges, and a smooth guest checkout. Our guide to [checkout forms and guest checkout](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-checkout-form-guest-checkout-2026/) covers the build side.

**Trust and legal pages.** Shoppers who do not know you look for proof you are real: contact details, policies, a grievance contact. Our guide to [legal and trust pages for an Indian store](/blog/gst-registration-shopify-woocommerce/) lists what to display.

**Speed.** Store pages need to be fast on mid-range phones. See [store speed and Core Web Vitals](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-store-speed-core-web-vitals-2026/).

**Shipping and order handling.** Connecting a courier, showing delivery estimates and sending tracking updates. Our article on [connecting shipping to your website](/blog/choose-ecommerce-logistics-partner/) covers the website side.

**Traffic.** The big one. You need a plan for how visitors will arrive: search engine optimisation, Google Ads, Meta ads, email, WhatsApp, social media and referrals. A store without a traffic plan is a shop without a street.

The first seven are things a developer builds. The last is something the business, perhaps with an agency, must sustain. Many failed stores had a good build and no traffic plan.

### The cost question, handled honestly

People ask "how much does an ecommerce website cost in Pune?" and the honest answer is that it depends on the platform, the catalogue size, the design effort and the integrations. TODO: insert a sourced price range after collecting at least three written quotes for a clearly defined scope. Market ranges can be wide, from template-based stores at the low end to custom builds at the high end.

More useful than a headline price is the shape of the cost.

- **One-off build:** design, setup, product upload, integrations, testing.
- **Recurring platform costs:** subscription fees or hosting, domain, apps or plugins, payment provider fees.
- **Recurring effort:** maintenance, content, support.
- **Traffic costs:** ads, content, agency fees, which are usually the largest ongoing item.

Compare this with the real cost of staying on marketplaces, which, as we noted, you can read from your own settlement reports. The decision is not "website cost versus nothing", but "own channel costs versus marketplace costs, over time".

### Mistakes we see most often

**Building a store before there is a plan to get visitors.** The store launches, a few friends visit, and then nothing. Decide the first three traffic sources before the build starts.

**Treating the store as a copy of the marketplace listing.** Copying thin marketplace text and images produces thin pages. Use the extra space and control to give buyers more.

**Ignoring the customer data advantage.** If you collect emails and WhatsApp opt-ins at checkout, with consent, you can reach customers again without paying a platform. If you do not, you have built a more expensive version of a marketplace listing.

**Leaving the marketplace entirely and too soon.** Some sellers abandon marketplaces in enthusiasm and lose their main source of orders before the own store has traffic. Move gradually and watch the numbers.

**Underestimating operations.** Delays and weak support online show up in reviews quickly. Make sure you can ship and respond before pushing traffic.

**Copying a competitor's site without understanding their model.** A large brand with heavy advertising and a vast catalogue works differently from a small seller with a focused range.

### Worked example: a Pune food brand deciding what to do

Take a hypothetical Pune-based maker of packaged snacks. This is an illustration, not a real client. They sell on two marketplaces, and a share of orders also come by WhatsApp from regular customers and local shops.

Looking at their settlement reports, they total all fees and returns and see the marketplaces take a considerable share of each sale. Looking at orders, they notice repeat buyers cluster around a few products, and WhatsApp customers reorder without prompting.

They decide not to leave the marketplaces. Instead they build a simple store on a platform their team can manage, with a limited catalogue: the products repeat buyers want, plus gift boxes available only on their own site. They add the store link to their WhatsApp catalogue and invoices, in line with marketplace rules, and add a reorder button for existing customers. They plan three traffic sources: existing WhatsApp contacts, local search for their locality and a modest Instagram effort.

The result is not guaranteed, and we do not claim figures. The point is the reasoning: they used the own store for the part where it has an advantage, repeat and direct orders, and kept the marketplaces for discovery.

### A decision checklist

Use this to decide whether to start.

1. I have totalled the real marketplace cost per sale from the last three months of data.
2. Some customers already search for my brand, or buy repeatedly.
3. I know my first three sources of traffic for an own store.
4. I can pack, ship and support orders reliably.
5. Someone is responsible for the store's content and updates each week.
6. I have read each marketplace's seller policy about customer contact and pricing.
7. I have a product list worth selling directly, including bundles or items marketplaces do not suit.
8. I have a budget for traffic, not only for the build.

If five or more are true, an own store is likely worth building. If fewer, strengthen the foundations or start with a very simple store while keeping marketplaces as the main channel.

### How to start without overbuilding

You do not need the full store at once. A sensible first version has a small catalogue, a clean product page template, a checkout with the payment methods your customers use, clear policies, and a way to capture email and WhatsApp consent. You can add subscriptions, wholesale pricing, reviews and wishlists later, as our guides on [subscription commerce](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-subscription-commerce-2026/) and [product reviews](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-product-reviews-ratings-system-2026/) describe.

Launch, watch the numbers for a few months, and let the data tell you what to build next.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is it better to sell on Amazon or on my own website?

Neither is better in general. Marketplaces give you buyers quickly but control the relationship and take fees. Your own website gives you control and customer data but you must bring the visitors. Many Indian sellers use both, with marketplaces for discovery and the own store for repeat and direct orders.

### Do I need my own website if I already sell on marketplaces?

Not always, but it becomes worthwhile when customers repeat, when people search for your brand, or when marketplace costs and rules limit you. Without a website, you cannot reach those customers directly and you depend on the marketplace for every sale.

### How much does it cost to build an ecommerce website in Pune?

It depends on the platform, catalogue size, design and integrations, so a single figure would mislead. Collect written quotes for a clearly defined scope and compare what each includes. Remember to budget for traffic, which is usually the biggest ongoing cost after the build.

### Can I promote my own website on marketplace listings?

Usually not directly. Most marketplaces restrict taking buyers off the platform, including in packaging and messages. Read each platform's seller policy and follow it. Use your own channels, such as WhatsApp, social media and your invoices where permitted, to build your direct audience.

### Should I price my own store lower than the marketplace?

Not automatically. Check each marketplace's pricing rules first. Many sellers keep prices consistent and give own-store buyers extras such as bundles, early access or better service, which avoids a price fight and protects margins.

## Where to Start

Start with your numbers: total marketplace costs per sale over the last three months, and the share of orders that come from repeat or direct customers. Then work through the checklist above. If the answer is yes, begin with a small first version and a clear traffic plan.
